subject: phy
title: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
syllabus: Dual nature of radiation; photoelectric effect; Hertz and Lenard's observations; Einstein's photoelectric equation; particle nature of light; matter waves — wave nature of particle, de Broglie relation.

body:
Light energy arrives in lumps called photons:
E = hν = \f{hc}{λ}, p = \f{h}{λ} = \f{E}{c}
Handy: E (in eV) = \f{1240}{λ (in nm)}. A 620 nm red photon carries 2 eV; a 310 nm UV photon 4 eV.
Photons have zero rest mass, always move at c and still carry momentum — that is why light exerts radiation pressure.

A source of power P emits
n = \f{P}{hν} = \f{Pλ}{hc} photons per second
— for the same power, LONGER wavelength means MORE photons.

body: Light shining on a metal can knock electrons out. Experiments found four facts the wave theory could not explain:
1) There is a threshold frequency ν_{0}: below it no electron comes out, however bright the light.
2) Above it, emission is instant (no time lag).
3) The maximum kinetic energy depends on FREQUENCY, not intensity.
4) The NUMBER of electrons (the saturation current) is proportional to intensity.
Stopping potential V_{0}: the retarding voltage that stops even the fastest electron, eV_{0} = K_{max}. It changes with frequency and the metal, never with intensity.

body:
One photon gives all its energy to one electron:
hν = φ + K_{max} = φ + eV_{0}
Work function φ = hν_{0} = \f{hc}{λ_{0}}: the least energy needed to free an electron (Cs ≈ 1.9 eV, Na ≈ 2.3–2.75 eV, Zn ≈ 4.3 eV).
Two wavelengths, two stopping potentials? Write the equation twice and SUBTRACT — φ cancels and hc/λ drops out.
Threshold wavelength λ_{0} = \f{1240}{φ (eV)} nm: only light SHORTER than λ_{0} works.

check.q: φ = 2 eV, light of 4 eV. Stopping potential?

body: K_{max} vs ν: straight line, slope = h, cuts the ν-axis at ν_{0}. Same slope for every metal (parallel lines).
V_{0} vs ν: straight line, slope = h/e; intercept on the V-axis = −φ/e (so φ can be found without h).
Current vs voltage: saturation current grows with intensity; all curves for one frequency meet the axis at the SAME −V_{0}. Higher frequency → larger V_{0}.
For the same light, the metal with the SMALLER work function (smaller ν_{0}) gives faster electrons.

body:
Every moving particle has a wave:
λ = \f{h}{p} = \f{h}{mv} = \f{h}{√{2mK}}

Accelerated from rest through V: K = qV → λ = \f{h}{√{2mqV}}. For an electron:
λ ≈ \f{1.227}{√{V}} nm
Same K → λ ∝ 1/√{m} (lighter = longer wave). Same λ → same momentum → K ∝ 1/m. Thermal particle: λ = \f{h}{√{3mkT}}.
Davisson–Germer: 54 V electrons diffracted from a nickel crystal like X-rays — direct proof of matter waves.

body: λ follows the SPEED: whatever changes v changes λ.
Magnetic field: force ⟂ velocity, no work, speed constant → λ unchanged.
Electric field along the motion (pushing the electron forward, i.e. E opposite to v): v = v_{0} + \f{eE}{m}t → λ falls.
Uniform field from rest: v = at → λ ∝ 1/t and dλ/dt ∝ 1/t^{2}.

formulas: K_{max}–ν slope h;  V_{0}–ν slope h/e
traps: Intensity changes the NUMBER of electrons, never their maximum energy.
Same power: longer wavelength → MORE photons per second.
K_{max}–ν slope is h; V_{0}–ν slope is h/e.
Angular frequency ω ≠ ν: E = hω/2π.
A magnetic field cannot change a particle's de Broglie wavelength.
Same de Broglie λ → same momentum, NOT the same energy.

pyq.q: The work function of a metal is 3 eV. The color of the visible light that is required to cause emission of photoelectrons is
sol: Threshold wavelength λ_{0} = \f{hc}{φ} = \f{1240 eV nm}{3 eV} ≈ 413 nm.
Only light with λ < 413 nm can eject electrons. Red (~700), yellow (~580) and green (~530 nm) are too long; blue/violet (~400–450 nm, its short end) works → Blue.

pyq.q: Assertion A: In photoelectric effect, on increasing the intensity of incident light the stopping potential increases. Reason R: Increase in intensity of light increases the rate of photoelectrons emitted, provided the frequency of incident light is greater than threshold frequency.
sol: Stopping potential depends only on frequency (eV_{0} = hν − φ), not on intensity → A is false.
More intensity = more photons per second = more photoelectrons per second (if ν > ν_{0}) → R is true.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false

pyq.q: Assertion A: Number of photons increases with increase in frequency of light. Reason R: Maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons increases with the frequency of incident radiation.
sol: For a fixed power, number of photons n = \f{P}{hν} FALLS as frequency rises → A is not correct.
K_{max} = hν − φ rises with ν → R is correct.
o: Both A and R are correct and R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is correct but R is not correct.
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is not correct but R is correct.

pyq.q: Which of the following statement is not true about stopping potential (V_{0})?
sol: eV_{0} = hν − φ: depends on the material (φ) and on frequency; V_{0} = K_{max}/e.
It does NOT depend on intensity → option 3 is not true.
o: It depends on the nature of emitter material.
It depends upon frequency of the incident light.
It increases with increase in intensity of the incident light.
It is 1/e times the maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted.

Which of the following phenomena does not explain by wave nature of light. (A) reflection (B) diffraction (C) photoelectric effect (D) interference (E) polarization
sol: Reflection, diffraction, interference and polarization are all explained by waves.
The photoelectric effect (instant emission, threshold frequency, K_{max} independent of intensity) needs photons → C only.

A proton and an electron have the same de Broglie wavelength. If K_{p} and K_{e} be the kinetic energies of proton and electron respectively. Then choose the correct relation :
sol: Same λ → same momentum p = h/λ.
K = \f{p^{2}}{2m}: the heavier proton has LESS kinetic energy → K_{p} < K_{e}.

sol: The wave contains two angular frequencies; the fastest photons have ω = 12 × 10^{15} rad/s.

The work functions of cesium (Cs) and lithium (Li) metals are 1.9 eV and 2.5 eV, respectively. If we incident a light of wavelength 550 nm on these two metal surfaces, then photo-electric effect is possible for the case of
sol: Emission needs hν ≥ φ: 2.25 > 1.9 (Cs ✓) but 2.25 < 2.5 (Li ✗) → Cs only.

pyq.q: A light source of wavelength λ illuminates a metal surface and electrons are ejected with maximum kinetic energy of 2 eV. If the same surface is illuminated by a light source of wavelength \f{λ}{2}, then the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons will be (The work function of metal is 1 eV)
sol: Half the wavelength → double the photon energy: 6 eV → K_{max} = 6 − 1 = 5 eV.

pyq.q: In photoelectric effect an em-wave is incident on a metal surface and electrons are ejected from the surface. If the work function of the metal is 2.14 eV and stopping potential is 2 V, what is the wavelength of the em-wave? (Given hc = 1242 eV nm where h is the Planck's constant and c is the speed of light in vaccum.)
An electron of mass 'm' with an initial velocity v = v_{0}î (v_{0} > 0) enters an electric field E = −E_{0}k̂. If the initial de Broglie wavelength is λ_{0}, the value after time t would be
sol: The force eE_{0} (along +z for the electron) is perpendicular to v_{0}: v_{x} = v_{0}, v_{z} = \f{eE_{0}t}{m}.

pyq.q: In photoelectric effect, the stopping potential (V_{0}) v/s frequency (ν) curve is plotted. (h is the Planck's constant and φ_{0} is work function of metal) (A) V_{0} v/s ν is linear. (B) The slope of V_{0} v/s ν curve = \f{φ_{0}}{h}. (C) h constant is related to the slope of V_{0} v/s ν line. (D) The value of electric charge of electron is not required to determine h using the V_{0} v/s ν curve. (E) The work function can be estimated without knowing the value of h.
sol: V_{0} = \f{h}{e}ν − \f{φ_{0}}{e}: a straight line (A ✓) with slope h/e (B ✗, C ✓).
Getting h from the slope needs e (D ✗).
The V-intercept is −φ_{0}/e, so φ_{0} follows without h (E ✓) → A, C, E.

pyq.q: A convex lens of focal length 40 cm forms an image of an extended source of light on a photoelectric cell. A current I is produced. The lens is replaced by another convex lens having the same diameter but focal length 20 cm. The photoelectric current now is :
sol: The light energy collected depends on the lens APERTURE (diameter), which is unchanged.
The same light power falls on the cell (the image is just smaller), so the current stays I.

Assertion (A): Emission of electrons in photoelectric effect can be suppressed by applying a sufficiently negative electron potential to the photo emissive substance. Reason (R): A negative electric potential, which stops the emission of electrons from the surface of a photo emissive substance, varies linearly with frequency of incident radiation.
sol: A large enough retarding potential stops even the fastest electrons → A true.
That stopping potential, V_{0} = (hν − φ)/e, is linear in ν → R true.
But R only describes how V_{0} depends on ν; it does not explain why emission can be suppressed → not the explanation.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Electromagnetic waves carry energy but not momentum. Reason (R): Mass of a photon is zero.
sol: EM waves carry momentum p = E/c (radiation pressure) → A false.
A photon has zero rest mass → R true.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

pyq.q: The work function of a substance is 3.0 eV. The longest wavelength of light that can cause the emission of photoelectrons from this substance is approximately:
For the photoelectric effect, the maximum kinetic energy (E_{k}) of the photoelectrons is plotted against the frequency (ν) of the incident photons. The slope of the graph gives
sol: E_{k} = hν − φ is a straight line in ν.
Its slope is h — Planck's constant. (The V_{0}–ν graph has slope h/e.)
o: Ratio of Planck's constant to electric charge

pyq.q: When a metal surface is illuminated by light of wavelength λ, the stopping potential is 8 V. When the same surface is illuminated by light of wavelength 3λ, stopping potential is 2 V. The threshold wavelength for this surface is :

In a photoelectric effect experiment a light of frequency 1.5 times the threshold frequency is made to fall on the surface of photosensitive material. Now if the frequency is halved and intensity is doubled, the number of photo electrons emitted will be:
sol: Below threshold no electron is emitted, however intense the light → zero.

pyq.q: The de Broglie wavelength associated with an electron accelerated through a potential difference V is λ_{e} and the de Broglie wavelength associated with a proton accelerated through the same potential difference is λ_{p}. If their corresponding masses are m_{e} and m_{p}, respectively, then the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths (\f{λ_{e}}{λ_{p}}) is ______.
sol: Both gain K = eV (same charge size).

pyq.q: Light is incident on a metallic plate having work function 110 × 10^{−20} J. If the produced photoelectrons have zero kinetic energy then the angular frequency of the incident light is ______ rad/s. (h = 6.63 × 10^{−34} J.s)

An electron of mass m is moving in an electric field E = −2E_{0}î (E_{0} = constant > 0), with an initial velocity V = v_{0}î (v_{0} = constant > 0). If λ_{0} = \f{h}{4mv_{0}}, its de Broglie wavelength at time t is ______. (e = charge of electron)
sol: Force on the electron F = −e(−2E_{0}î) = +2eE_{0}î — along its motion, so it speeds up: v = v_{0} + \f{2eE_{0}t}{m}.

sol: The sheet's field σ/2ε_{0} is uniform → constant acceleration a, so v = at.

pyq.q: A photo-emissive substance is illuminated with a radiation of wavelength λ_{i} so that it releases electrons with de-Broglie wavelength λ_{e}. The longest wavelength of radiation that can emit photoelectron is λ_{0}. Expression for de-Broglie wavelength is given by : (m : mass of the electron, h : Planck's constant and c : speed of light)

An electron with mass 'm' with an initial velocity (t = 0) v = v_{0}î (v_{0} > 0) enters a magnetic field B = B_{0}ĵ. If the initial de-Broglie wavelength at t = 0 is λ_{0} then its value after time 't' would be :
sol: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work: speed stays v_{0}.

pyq.q: Match List-I with List-II: (A) Planck's constant (B) Stopping potential (C) Work function (D) Threshold frequency — (I) ML^{2}T^{−2} (II) T^{−1} (III) ML^{2}T^{−1} (IV) ML^{2}T^{−3}A^{−1}
sol: h = E/ν → ML^{2}T^{−1} (III). Stopping potential is a voltage → ML^{2}T^{−3}A^{−1} (IV).
Work function is an energy → ML^{2}T^{−2} (I). Frequency → T^{−1} (II).
